Median CNR on QSM (P<0.05) relative to CM was highest for medial pulvinar (median 2.9, interquartile range 1.6-4.7) and ventral lateral thalamus (1.6, 0.6-2.3). Highest overall CNR was seen on WMn for PuM (3.4, 3.0-4.0). SNR on QSM was highest for anterior pulvinar (2.4, 1.1-3.6) and highest overall SNR was on on MP2RAGE for PuA (20.8, 17.3-24.3). In an indirect comparison across independent cohorts, QSM showed greater lateral thalamic contrast than WMn and MP2RAGE, but lower overall SNR. Conclusion QSM allows visualization of CM including the lateral border poorly seen on other sequences, and may be useful as a complementary sequence for direct targeting of CM.

item.title: Vascular dementia and vascular cognitive impairment-current treatments and future prospects.
item.description:
International journal of stroke : official journal of the International Stroke Society
Vascular cognitive impairment (VCI) and vascular dementia (VaD) represent a substantial and growing global health burden, yet remain under-recognized and comparatively under-researched. Two broad categories are post-stroke cognitive impairment, and VCI secondary to chronic cerebrovascular disease of which the most common cause is cerebral small vessel disease (SVD). In addition, cerebrovascular pathology frequently coexists with Alzheimer's disease (AD), increasing the probability that AD pathology will manifest as clinical dementia. Current management focuses primarily on prevention through modification of cardiovascular risk factors and lifestyle interventions. Intensive blood-pressure control has shown the strongest evidence, reducing future all-cause dementia while slowing progression of white-matter abnormalities. Multidomain lifestyle interventions incorporating exercise, diet, cognitive training, and vascular risk monitoring may also preserve cognition, although results across trials remain variable. In established VCI and VaD, treatment options are limited; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine lack convincing evidence of benefit, and no pharmacological therapy has definitively demonstrated symptomatic improvement or delayed disease progression. Advances in understanding SVD and VCI pathophysiology are, however, identifying promising therapeutic targets. Emerging evidence highlights endothelial dysfunction, impaired cerebral autoregulation, increased blood-brain barrier permeability, inflammation, and glymphatic dysfunction as possible mechanisms underlying SVD. Current trials are evaluating treatment approaches based on this framework including cerebral vasodilators such as cilostazol, isosorbide mononitrate and phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, anti-inflammatory therapies, glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists, remote ischemic conditioning, and strategies targeting glymphatic function. Improved mechanistic understanding, appropriately targeted interventions, and adequately powered long-term clinical trials are required to translate these emerging approaches into effective treatments for VCI and VaD.

item.title: Predicting trail-making test performance using 7-Tesla structural cerebral MRI.
item.description:
Translational psychiatry
Psychopharmaceutical therapy has seen a lack of improvement in efficacy, highlighting the need for a more individualized treatment approach that optimally leverages pharmaceutical effects. To achieve this, it is necessary to identify factors that can predict psychological attributes and treatment outcomes. We hypothesize that brain morphology may serve as a predictor of performance in psychological tests. A 7-Tesla-MRI system was used to measure 74 transdiagnostic patients and 41 healthy controls. Values for grey matter volume (GMV), cortical thickness and gyrification based on the Schaefer 100 Atlas for parcellation were determined. Using this morphological data, performance in a Trail-Making Test (TMT) - A and B was predicted with the help of a deep learning model. A SHAP analysis was conducted to identify the key variables important for the model. The accuracy in predicting TMT performance was very good at 0.795. The most decisive feature influencing predictions was gyrification. Areas indicating inter-group differences were focused in the frontal cortex, as well as in temporal and parietal regions. Morphological characteristics can predict test performance with high accuracy. These results support the implementation of a transdiagnostic approach in clinical practice to better address the underlying pathophysiology. Symptom prediction based on neuroimaging data appears to be an achievable goal.

item.title: A shape deformation-based framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Individualized morphological brain networks have emerged as an important framework for imaging-based connectomics. However, existing methods have focused predominantly on the cerebral cortex, leaving subcortical structures largely unexplored despite their central roles in cognition and neuropsychiatric disorders. Here, we developed a novel framework for constructing individualized subcortical morphological networks from structural magnetic resonance imaging. Specifically, subcortical surfaces were reconstructed using a Point2Mesh-optimized multilayer perceptron architecture and vertex-wise shape deformation was quantified as the signed Euclidean distance between each vertex on an individual mesh and the corresponding vertex on the group-average template mesh. Interregional morphological connectivity in local shape deformation distributions was subsequently estimated using Jensen-Shannon Divergence. Applying this approach to the Human Connectome Project dataset, we found that subcortical morphological networks exhibited complex topological organization, including small-world architecture, modular organization, and highly connected hubs, which were consistently preserved at finer subregional scales. Analyses using an independent test-retest dataset further demonstrated fair-to-good reliability of these network properties. Importantly, these shape deformation-based networks showed significant coupling with subcortical functional networks estimated from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Leveraging large-scale multisite clinical datasets, we further demonstrated alterations of subcortical morphological networks in schizophrenia and major depressive disorder. Schizophrenia was characterized predominantly by right caudate-centered disruptions in morphological connectivity and nodal centrality, whereas major depressive disorder exhibited alterations only in nodal centrality of the right amygdala. Together, these findings establish a novel and reliable framework for investigating subcortical morphological network organization in the human brain across both healthy and psychiatric populations.

item.title: Multivariate prediction of white matter BOLD activity and its relationship to marginal connectivity.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Functional MRI studies have traditionally focused on gray matter, whereas white matter BOLD signals have often been treated as weak or artifactual. However, white matter BOLD fluctuations are robustly detectable and contain reproducible functional information, yet most gray-to-white matter analyses rely on only marginal functional connectivity, which cannot separate pairwise coupling from shared variance among distributed cortical systems. Here, we used a multivariate cortical prediction framework to test whether spontaneous white matter BOLD activity can be predicted from distributed cortical gray matter BOLD activity, and how this predictive structure relates to marginal connectivity. Resting-state fMRI data from 81 Human Connectome Project young adult participants were analyzed using a strict white matter mask with no overlap with cortical predictors. For each white matter voxel, time series from 400 cortical parcels were used to predict white matter BOLD signals with nested leave-one-run-out ridge regression. Cortical BOLD activity modestly but reliably predicted white matter BOLD dynamics, demonstrating consistent cross-validated prediction accuracy across a broad spatial extent of the white matter. Ridge β coefficients strongly recapitulated marginal functional connectivity fingerprints, indicating a shared functional backbone, but their first gradients differed reproducibly. The difference between these gradients defined a β-minus-FC G1 divergence axis that remained stable after broadly controlling for anatomical, signal-related, and spatial factors. At the low end of the axis, enriched in callosal and capsular structures, pairwise gray-to-white matter connectivity was relatively strong, but white matter BOLD fluctuations were predicted less well by distributed cortical BOLD activity than that connectivity would suggest. At the high end, enriched in posterior projection and association pathways, pairwise connectivity was relatively weak, but distributed cortical BOLD activity predicted white matter BOLD signals better than expected. These findings identify a reproducible, tract-organized contrast between marginal connectivity and its covariance-adjusted predictive representation.

item.title: Reduced Somatomotor Cortical Thickness in Women With PTSD After Childhood Sexual Abuse: A Structural Correlate Distinct From Adult Sexual Dysfunction.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Background Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is a major risk factor for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and adult sexual dysfunction in women. Although adverse childhood experiences have been linked to altered brain structure, cortical alterations specifically associated with CSA and PTSD in women remain poorly characterized, and their relationship to adult sexual functioning is unknown. Methods Women with CSA and current PTSD (n = 52), women with CSA without current PTSD (n = 32), and control women without CSA or PTSD (n = 48) underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging. Cortical thickness, surface area, and cortical volume were examined using whole brain vertex wise analyses. Sexual functioning was assessed in a subsample (n = 41). Results Women with CSA and current PTSD showed reduced cortical thickness within a left somatomotor cluster relative to controls (cluster wise p = .017). Anatomical characterization localized the cluster to motor and premotor regions involved in bodily self representation and sensorimotor integration. No group differences were observed in cortical surface area or volume. Women with CSA and PTSD also reported lower sexual functioning, particularly in arousal, lubrication, satisfaction and pain. Cortical thickness within the somatomotor cluster was unrelated to sexual functioning and did not mediate the association between CSA severity and sexual dysfunction. Conclusions These findings suggest that somatomotor cortical alterations represent neurobiological correlates of trauma related psychopathology following CSA in women. The absence of associations with adult sexual functioning suggests that structural alterations within the somatomotor cortex may be distinct from mechanisms contributing to sexual dysfunction.

item.title: Sex shapes capillary flows and oxygen extraction in the middle-aged mouse brain
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Sex differences in brain aging are well documented, but their origin within the cerebrovascular hierarchy remains unclear. Here we show that cortical blood flow is higher in female than male mice at 15 months of age, at a point when an earlier sex difference in pulsatility and resistance indices has already converged, pial vessel diameter shows no difference between sexes, and estrogen levels are similar between sexes. Using an indicator-dilution and intravascular oxygen measurements using two-photon microscopy, we found that capillary transit-time heterogeneity (CTH) scales more steeply with mean transit time in females, consistent with a passively regulated capillary network, and that this is accompanied by reduced oxygen extraction fraction (OEF) without deficit in arterial oxygen delivery. Spatial transcriptomics reveals that sex differences are organized into distinct regional programs, most prominently in white matter, where a male-associated myelin and axonogenesis signature accompanies reduced white matter volume in females. These molecular and structural differences coincide with elevated hippocampal microglial reactivity and an altered spatial search strategy in females, without any detectable differences in circulating markers of stress, blood-brain barrier integrity, or immunity. Together, these findings indicate that sex differences in the aging brain are expressed at the level of capillary flow regulation and regional tissue programs rather than through bulk cerebral blood flow alone, and that elevated blood flow in females can mask, rather than reflect, adequate tissue oxygenation.

item.title: Long-term memory and microstructural changes after chemotherapy and low-dose radiotherapy covering the whole ventricle in patients with germinoma
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Purpose This study assessed memory impairment and underlying microstructural changes in patients with germinoma treated long-term with 24 Gy radiation, which covered the whole ventricle, with chemotherapy (low-dose WVI with chemotherapy). Methods This prospective observational study included patients treated with low-dose WVI with chemotherapy at our departments from 1999 to 2021. Their intelligence and memory were assessed using the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale, 3rd Edition, and the Wechsler Memory Scale, Revised Edition (WMS-R). Diffusion tensor images (DTI) and neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) metrics were calculated in white and gray matter and compared to the mean values from 11 age-matched healthy individuals. Associations between DTI and NODDI metrics and WMS-R memory scores were also examined. Results Among 68 patients treated with low-dose WVI with chemotherapy, 32 provided consent for evaluation. The median ages at treatment and evaluation were 17.1 and 24.9 years, respectively. Sixteen (50%) patients had WMS-R index scores below 85 (− 1 standard deviation). Memory was more severely impaired than intelligence or attention. DTI and NODDI metrics showed alterations in extensive gray and white matter regions associated with memory. DTI and NODDI metrics in the fornix, cingulum, cingulate cortex, orbital cortex, and thalamus correlated with memory scores. Conclusion Memory impairment is common in these patients, with microstructural changes in extensive memory-related regions associated with impaired memory function.

item.title: Adaptive local region super-resolution for high-field MRI: A diffusion-based approach with structural and frequency-domain constraints.
item.description:
Magnetic resonance imaging
High-field MRI offers superior SNR but is constrained by the trade-off between spatial resolution and acquisition time. Existing global deep learning super-resolution (SR) methods often incur computational overhead by ignoring regional image content. This motivates an adaptive local SR strategy to optimize efficiency and detail preservation. To address this, we developed a local SR method that adaptively allocates computational resources to information-rich regions. The proposed framework regularized an entropy-based local region processing strategy with a diffusion model fortified by frequency-domain and structural constraints. We retrospectively evaluated our method on two diverse datasets: a proprietary 7.0 T dental MRI dataset (25 T2-weighted DESS sequences from 10 beagle dogs) and a public 5.0 T brain MRI dataset (Diff5T, 50 diffusion-weighted sequences). Image quality was quantified using PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and FID. On the 7.0 T dental test dataset (2 subjects), our method achieved a PSNR of 27.31 [26.83, 27.79] dB and the lowest LPIPS of 0.19 [0.18, 0.20]. On the 5.0 T brain test dataset (10 subjects), the method achieved a PSNR of 27.15 ± 0.10 dB, an LPIPS of 0.14 ± 0.00 and an FID of 54.01, with lower perceptual metrics than the evaluated baselines. Ablation studies indicated that the proposed frequency-domain and structural constraints reduced LPIPS and FID, with trade-offs in PSNR and SSIM. In conclusion, the evaluated framework showed improvements in perceptual metrics by integrating targeted local processing with frequency-domain and structural regularization, accompanied by a trade-off in pixel-wise fidelity metrics, supporting the technical feasibility of addressing the resolution-time trade-off in high-field MRI. Future work will focus on expanding the dataset and evaluating the framework in human dental cohorts to address anatomical differences between the current canine model and human dental anatomy.

item.title: Prenatal exposure to PFAS and multimodal structural brain development across childhood.
item.description:
Environment international
Background Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are ubiquitous environmental pollutants that are posited to be neurotoxic to the developing brain; however, the impact of prenatal exposure to PFAS - particularly to newer, short-chain PFAS - on brain development across childhood is unclear. Methods Concentrations of 9 PFAS were quantified in cord blood plasma of 452 infants (440 for the diffusion sample) who later participated in structural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at ages 4.5, 6, 7.5, and 10.5 years, providing estimates of regional cortical thickness and surface area, subcortical volumes, and fractional anisotropy (FA) of key white matter tracts. Longitudinal mixed-effect models estimated associations of PFAS with age 4.5 brain metrics and their developmental trajectories across childhood after correcting for the false discovery rate within PFAS and outcome domains. Results Higher concentrations of PFNA and PFDA in cord blood were associated with lower model-estimated age 4.5 surface area of the right paracentral lobule. PFHpA was associated with faster surface area growth in the left rostral anterior cingulate and slower growth in the right caudal middle frontal gyrus from 4.5 to 10.5 years. The short-chain compound PFBS was linked with greater model-estimated age 4.5 FA in 12 white matter tracts, while PFOA and PFNA were linked with lower FA in the middle cerebellar peduncle and the left corticospinal tract, respectively. Associations of PFBS with FA attenuated with age in several tracts. Conclusions Prenatal exposure to PFAS was associated with altered development of frontal and paracentral regions and of white matter microstructure. These findings highlight the need for further research examining the long-term associations of prenatal exposure to PFAS with children's neurodevelopment.

item.title: Animal models for investigating post-stroke cognitive impairment: A neurovascular trafficking perspective.
item.description:
Animal models and experimental medicine
Post-stroke cognitive impairment (PSCI) is a major cause of long-term disability after ischemic stroke, yet its mechanisms remain incompletely explained by infarct volume, lesion location, or conventional vascular risk factors alone. Animal models are indispensable for clarifying how ischemic injury evolves into delayed cognitive dysfunction and for determining which mechanisms are experimentally tractable, reproducible, and translationally relevant. This review examines PSCI from a neurovascular trafficking perspective, focusing on how laboratory animal models can be used to investigate secretory pathway stress, endolysosomal dysfunction, autophagy-lysosomal flux, extracellular vesicle signaling, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial reactivity, myelin debris clearance, white matter injury, and cognition-relevant behavioral phenotypes. Rodent models of transient or permanent middle cerebral artery occlusion, photothrombotic stroke, embolic stroke, chronic cerebral hypoperfusion, bilateral carotid artery stenosis, and subcortical white-matter injury each reproduce selected components of the human PSCI spectrum. No single model fully captures the temporal, vascular, cellular, and cognitive complexity of human PSCI; therefore, model selection should be driven by the mechanistic question, disease phase, vascular pathology, cellular compartment, cognitive domain, and welfare burden under investigation. The central argument is not that neurovascular trafficking failure is already a proven causal pathway, but that well-designed animal studies can test, refine, or falsify this hypothesis. Future studies should integrate model validity, translational rigor, and welfare refinement through longitudinal cognitive testing, multimodal imaging, cell-specific molecular profiling, extracellular vesicle phenotyping, intervention-based validation, randomization, blinding, sample-size justification, humane endpoints, perioperative care, and transparent reporting.

item.title: MRI-based correlation of cry acoustic parameters and brain structural development in preterm infants.
item.description:
Acta psychologica
Objective Infant crying conveys abundant information, including neurophysiological, pathological, and psychological aspects. However, the relationship between crying and brain structure remains poorly understood. Methods In this study, 154 preterm infants and 84 term infants were enrolled, and their cries were recorded for 1 min under similar stimulation conditions. MATLAB software was used to analyse the crying data, for statistical analyses, repeated cry-level observations were averaged within infant, and each infant contributed one value for each cry acoustic parameter. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed in 43 preterm infants to measure the volumes of grey matter, white matter, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Results Preterm infants had longer cry cycle and inhale durations than term infants (P = 0.022 and 0.014). Among preterm infants, cry parameters did not differ significantly across gestational ages (all P > 0.05). In 43 preterm infants with MRI, grey and white matter volumes differed significantly across gestational age groups (P = 0.01 and 0.02), as did the grey matter/CSF and white matter/CSF ratios (P = 0.010 and 0.020). Correlations between cry parameters and brain volumes were generally weak. Multiple linear regression showed that cry parameters were associated with white matter volume (R2 = 0.38, P = 0.039) but not with grey matter or CSF volume. Conclusion This study identified associations between cry characteristics and MRI-derived brain volumes in infants across gestational ages. Although these findings suggest that cry characteristics may reflect certain aspects of brain development, the observed associations were generally weak and should be considered exploratory.

item.title: MRI and proton MR spectroscopy in neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy: a comprehensive imaging review.
item.description:
Japanese journal of radiology
Neonatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy (HIE) remains a leading cause of neonatal mortality and long-term neurodevelopmental disability. Although cranial ultrasound is widely used as a bedside screening tool, brain MRI has become central to diagnosis, injury pattern classification, timing estimation, and outcome prediction. Furthermore, proton MR spectroscopy (1 H-MRS) provides complementary metabolic biomarkers that enhance prognostication. This review focuses on MRI and 1 H-MRS in neonatal encephalopathy due to hypoxic-ischemic injury, addressing both term and preterm infants. The pathophysiologic determinants of injury distribution are summarized, the optimal timing of imaging and diffusion evolution is discussed, and practical acquisition protocols including recommended sequences and 1 H-MRS parameters are proposed. Key MRI phenotypes in term infants-basal ganglia-thalamus injury, watershed/parasagittal cortical-subcortical injury, and global or near-total injury patterns are reviewed with attention to common pitfalls such as diffusion pseudonormalization and evolving T1/T2 signal changes. For preterm infants, this review highlights distinctive vulnerabilities of the germinal matrix and periventricular white matter, emphasizing the spectrum from punctate white matter injury (WMI) to cystic periventricular leukomalacia (PVL). For 1 H-MRS, voxel selection, echo time considerations, and interpretation of lactate, N-acetylaspartate (NAA), choline, creatine, and myo-inositol are detailed. Evidence suggests that deep gray matter lactate/NAA or NAA-based metrics serve as reliable and robust outcome biomarkers. Emerging directions including arterial spin labeling (ASL) perfusion are also discussed.

item.title: Anatomical and radiological analysis of ventricular catheter trajectories: neuronavigation-guided dissection and tractography-based 3D visualization.
item.description:
Neurosurgical review
Ventricular catheter placement (VCP) is a life-saving intervention frequently performed in emergency departments and intensive care units. The free hand technique is the most commonly used approach for placing catheters. This study demonstrates the anatomical and radiological relationship between catheters inserted through the most commonly used access points and the anatomical structures in their path. Moreover, we calculate the insertion angles and catheter lengths that should be specified during VCP. Six donated human heads, fixed in 10% formalin and injected with colored silicone dye, were used in this study. Ventricular catheters were inserted through Kocher's, Paine's, Keen's, Frazier's, and Dandy's points under navigation. Dissection was performed from the skin to the inner wall of the ventricle while preserving the inserted catheters. The insertion angle and delivery length for each access point were measured both in the donated human heads and in 50 patients with hydrocephalus. In addition, magnetic resonance tractography was performed, and the relationship of each catheter with anatomical structures was presented as a three-dimensional model. Catheters inserted from Keen's and Paine's points pass through regions containing dense and crucial vascular structures. Catheters inserted from Keen's, Paine's, and Frazier's points enter the cortex through eloquent areas. The catheter inserted from Keen's point passes through the most diverse white matter pathway. Catheters inserted from Kocher's and Dandy's points pass through regions with less dense cortical vascular structures. Moreover, they pass through noneloquent cortical structures and fewer white matter tracts. This is the first anatomical dissection and tractography report describing the relationship between catheters introduced through the most common ventricular access sites and the anatomical structures along their path from the skin to the ventricle. Understanding the anatomical and radiological three-dimensionality of VCP will increase the safety of its applications.

item.title: Facial emotion recognition of sadness relates to superior parietal gray matter volume in mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is associated with early, regionally selective neurodegenerative changes that may affect socioemotional functioning before atrophy becomes widespread. This study examined whether structural brain alterations in MCI relate to facial emotion recognition performance. Sixty adults (30 MCI, 30 healthy controls), aged 50-86 years, completed neuropsychological testing, the Facial emotion composite Task, and structural MRI. Whole-brain voxel-based morphometry revealed no significant gray matter volume differences between groups. However, targeted region-of-interest ROI analyses demonstrated lower right amygdala and bilateral hippocampal volumes in patients with MCI. Cortical thickness analyses identified two regions with lower thickness in MCI: the right superior parietal lobule and the left posterior insula. A significant Group × Sadness interaction indicated that the association between left superior parietal gray matter volume and sadness recognition differed between groups. Follow-up analyses of the extracted values showed a positive association in MCI, although this within-group association did not reach statistical significance, and a significant inverse association in HCs. These findings suggest that early MCI involves selective thinning in association cortices supporting attention and salience processing. The sadness-specific interaction indicates that patients with MCI may rely on preserved superior parietal structure during sadness recognition, a pattern that is consistent with structural reserve accounts, although this interpretation remains speculative given the cross-sectional design.

item.title: Frequency-dependent, asymmetric, and dynamic alterations of white matter function in primary hemifacial spasm: a multiband resting-state fMRI study.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Primary hemifacial spasm involves central network reorganization, but white matter functional alterations remain unclear. We acquired resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 89 left-sided patients, 92 right-sided patients, and 124 healthy controls. Patients exhibited widespread abnormalities in tracts including the corpus callosum, superior longitudinal fasciculus, and corona radiata. Notably, this remodeling was highly asymmetric: left-sided patients primarily showed increased local neural activity in prefrontal pathways, whereas right-sided patients exhibited increased global network centrality across interhemispheric tracts. Furthermore, these alterations displayed distinct frequency preferences, and certain functional instabilities were exclusively captured by dynamic metrics rather than static analyses. These findings demonstrate that the disorder is associated with time-varying, frequency-specific, and asymmetric white matter functional reorganization, highlighting the value of dynamic and multi-frequency approaches in decoding its pathophysiology.
